column3: The people of Hell call on their Lord for relief, but the mediated plea and no stated answer contrast with the focus's open promise.
God's call receives an answering response at resurrection, directly echoing the focus's call-and-response relation.
The summoned partners cannot answer their callers, exposing the false address that the focus excludes.
Those nearest to God do not grow proud of His worship but glorify and prostrate, the direct opposite of the focus's warning.
This nearby verse identifies baseless disputation with the pride that blocks receptive relation to God.
Mocking every messenger depicts rejection of divine address, though prayer and worship are not explicit.
The challenge to call alleged partners tests their inability to answer, sharply contrasting God's promised response.
The question exposes the object of inherited worship, preparing the false-worship alternative to the focus's exclusive address.
At punishment the wrongdoers promise to answer the call and follow messengers, showing a response deferred beyond its useful time.
Heavenly beings do not disdain God's worship, directly opposing the proud refusal named in the focus.
Refusal when God alone is invoked identifies the same rejection of exclusive divine address within the surah.
Exclusive worship and seeking help state the faithful posture toward God that the focus commands.
God explicitly answers the caller who calls on Him and asks people to answer Him in return, closely paralleling the focus.
Persistent worship of idols supplies the alternative allegiance that makes a true divine response impossible.
The resurrection reply joins certainty with being brought low, directly matching the focus's humiliated entry motif.
God answers a distressed appeal with concrete help, illustrating answered supplication without the worship-pride consequence.
The book's descent from God does not clarify calling, worship, pride, or entry into Hell.
All creatures come to God subdued after the trumpet, closely matching the focus's compelled humiliation.
Moses addresses his Lord for forgiveness and entry into mercy, a genuine prayer but without the focus's response or pride contrast.
The question whether idols hear when called directly tests the receiver's capacity that God affirms in the focus.
Refusal to worship what others worship marks separation from false worship, but lacks the call-and-answer structure.
Pride when told God's exclusive oneness shows the same resistance to divine summons that the focus condemns.
The verse links arrogant, tyrannical hearts to resistance against God's signs, supplying the immediate context for the focus's pride.
The judgment question asks what answer was given to the messengers, making response to divine address accountable.
Believers prostrate and praise when reminded of God's signs and do not act proudly, directly reversing the focus's condemned posture.
Sealed hearts, hearing, and sight suggest closed receptivity, but no call, worship, or humbled entry is stated.
Hell calls the one who turned away, reversing the refused summons into an unavoidable punitive call.
All creatures and angels prostrate to God without pride, directly contrasting refusal of His worship.
Within the same discourse, competing calls lead respectively to salvation and the Fire, clarifying the stakes of answer and refusal.
Those called besides God possess nothing, establishing why divine rather than rival address is effective.
The damned are driven to Hell after acknowledging ignored messengers, connecting rejected warning with the destination in the focus.
A prayer is declared answered while its speakers are told to remain steadfast, showing that response entails continued obligation.
Responding to God and the messenger after injury shows active receptivity to divine summons, though not prayer specifically.
Solomon's prayer for gratitude and entry among righteous servants is a genuine appeal but only indirectly relates to the focus.
God's provision of night and day and human ingratitude do not directly develop the focus's call, worship, or punishment sequence.
Noah's continual call to his people illustrates persistent prophetic address without an answering relation.
People answer Satan's call instead of God's truth and find no mutual rescue at judgment, a decisive contrast with the focus's promise.
The proud are commanded to enter Hell's gates, nearly repeating the focus's final judgment on arrogant worship-refusers.
The messenger calls people to believe in their Lord, placing faith as the needed response to a divine summons.
The Lord answers the believers and promises admission to gardens, the positive counterpart to the focus's unanswered pride and Hell.
This nearby judgment scene denies wrongdoers any useful excuse and assigns them an evil abode, reinforcing the focus's consequence.
Believers answer their Lord and embody that response through prayer, consultation, and giving.
The verse ends with disbelievers gathered to Hell, but their spending and obstruction do not clarify the focus's relation.
The question whether idols can benefit or harm completes the test of whether false objects can rightly receive worship and calls.
Repeated cries for destruction in Hell cannot alter the punishment, contrasting with the focus's prior invitation to call God.
The sign of Saul's kingship and the Ark do not develop the focus's themes.
The nearby assurance of God's true promise and return to Him gives broad judgment context but no specific call or worship link.
False addressees neither hear nor answer calls and repudiate association at judgment, the exact negative counterpart to the focus.
The hypocrites' oaths and Hell abode offer a general punishment parallel without call or worship dynamics.
On the Day all follow the Caller without deviation and voices are humbled, echoing the focus's ultimate compelled submission.
The community's call to good extends the pattern of summons and response, though it is not divine supplication.
Shu'ayb calls his people to worship God alone and warns of punishment, directly framing the choice behind the focus.
The proud are commanded to enter Hell's gates, an immediate verbal and thematic parallel to the focus's conclusion.
God asks the messengers what answer they received, making human response to revealed address a judgment issue.
An invitation and permitted entry concern household etiquette rather than divine calling, worship, or final judgment.
Whoever does not answer God's caller cannot escape or find protectors, closely expressing the peril of refusal.
Zechariah calls upon his Lord as the Hearer of prayer, a focused example of supplication without its stated answer.
Entry among God's servants gives a positive counterpart to the focus's entry into Hell after refusing worship.
Creation, form, provision, and praise of God do not directly develop the focus's relational sequence.
The Lord answers Joseph's plea and turns harm away, a concrete instance of the divine response promised in the focus.
Secret sinful speech culminates in Hell but does not meaningfully illuminate calling, worship, or pride.
The one Lord commands the united community to worship Him, stating the exclusive worship that pride refuses in the focus.
In the same surah, alleged partners vanish and the callers disown their prior calls, confirming the collapse of rival address.
Created things prostrate to God while subdued, combining worship and humbled posture in direct contrast to proud refusal.
The believer contrasts their call to disbelief and association with his call to the Mighty Forgiver, immediately clarifying the focus's address.
Noah commands worship of God alone and warns of painful punishment, supplying the same basic alternative as the focus.
Those following Satan receive Hell as their recompense, linking false allegiance to the destination warned in the focus.
Believers hear a caller to faith, answer with belief, and then pray to their Lord, closely modeling receptive response.
The community answers Lot's rebuke by expelling his family, a hostile response but not one focused on worship or prayer.
God's servants pray for Hell's punishment to be turned away, a sincere appeal set against the focus's doomed arrogance.
The same-surah contrast of punishment and garden entry supplies broad outcome context but lacks the focus's call or worship relation.
God addresses believing servants and commands exclusive worship of Him, directly opposing the focus's refusal of worship.
Iblis and his followers are promised a filled Hell after his expulsion, connecting proud rebellion with the focus's final humiliation.
Worshippers and the objects worshipped besides God enter Hell together, showing the consequence of diverted worship.
The people answer moral rebuke by demanding punishment, a defiant reply but only indirectly related to the focus.
Refusal and pride toward God's worship lead to compulsory gathering before Him, directly anticipating the focus's coerced outcome.
The stages of human creation and lifespan do not clarify the focus's call-and-answer or worship-pride relation.
Noah intensifies his public call, illustrating prophetic summons without the focus's divine response.
The proud are ordered into Hell's gates to remain there, closely matching the focus's threatened entry.
False gods and their worshippers remain eternally in Hell, reinforcing the judgment of misdirected worship.
God responds to believers who do good and increases His favor, the positive response contrasted with severe punishment for disbelievers.
Hell is made a confinement for disbelievers who return to wrongdoing, providing a general consequence parallel.
The woman's invitation and Joseph's refusal concern temptation rather than divine calling or worship.
Failure to answer the challenge supports God's exclusive knowledge and oneness, but the call is a proof challenge rather than supplication.
Associating another god leads to blame and expulsion into Hell, a related consequence though pride and worship refusal are not explicit.
The inhabitants of Hell cannot hear there, a limited contrast with the God who hears and answers calls.
Creation is expressly ordered toward worship of God, supplying the positive purpose rejected by the proud in the focus.
People are commanded to call their Lord humbly and privately, directly opposing arrogant worship refusal.
The dispersing winds do not clarify any of the focus's themes.
Human relationships carry competing calls toward Fire or toward garden and forgiveness, making the direction of summons consequential.
Those who hold fast to God are admitted into mercy and guided to Him, a positive entry outcome after faithful attachment.
The inhabitants of Paradise make praise their regular call, a distant positive contrast to petitions under threat.
Moses' rebuke of his people and dispute with Aaron do not develop the focus's call, worship, or judgment sequence.
The prohibition against calling powerless beings besides God directly confirms that only the true divine addressee should be invoked.
Human creation in stages has no material connection to the focus's themes.
Joseph contrasts prison with an immoral invitation and prays for protection, but the calling is not a divine summons.
The creation and ordering of earth and heavens do not clarify the focus's relational themes.
Abraham asks his people to reconsider what they worship, reopening false worship to the scrutiny implicit in the focus.
The warning of gradual reprieve for deniers lacks a meaningful call, worship, or humbled-entry connection.
Abraham's people answer his message with an order to kill or burn him, showing hostile refusal but not the focus's specific relation.
God is declared the shared Lord and explicitly commanded to be worshipped, stating the allegiance pride rejects in the focus.
The covenantal summons is to worship none but God and associate nothing with Him, directly governing rightful worship.
The command to worship God and associate nothing with Him gives the positive rule opposed by misdirected invocation and pride.
Those who invoke beings besides God are shown to be invoking Satan, directly contrasting exclusive divine address.
Those too proud for God's worship face punishment, closely matching the focus's warning against proud refusal.
Jesus calls people to worship God, and associating partners is paired with exclusion from Paradise and the Fire.
The challenge rejects worship of what cannot harm or benefit, directly supporting exclusive invocation of God.
Jesus' message is summarized as worshipping God, his Lord and theirs, a direct formulation of the focus's worship relation.
In overwhelming distress, people are asked whether they would call anyone but God, centering exclusive recourse.
People call God alone in distress and He removes the harm if He wills, a clear instance of effective divine response.
Those who call upon their Lord morning and evening model persistent devotion, though no answer is stated.
The Prophet is forbidden to worship those invoked besides God, reinforcing the boundary around true worship.
People call God sincerely for rescue from darkness and danger, a direct supplication scene.
Calling what cannot benefit or harm is rejected as reversal after guidance, directly contrasting the focus's proper addressee.
People are commanded to call on God with devotion made sincere and to worship as they began, closely joining invocation and worship.
The people resist abandoning named objects of worship, displaying the false allegiance opposed by the focus.
Alleged partners cannot create and are themselves created, undermining their fitness for worship or invocation.
False objects cannot answer a call to guidance, directly opposing God's responsive address.
Those invoked besides God cannot help their callers or help themselves, directly confirming the focus's exclusive relation.
Taking religious authorities as lords is contrasted with the command to worship one God alone.
A person calls upon God under affliction and then turns away after relief, showing a failed response to divine aid.
People call God with sincere devotion amid danger, illustrating direct recourse to Him alone.
Only God can remove harm or grant good, supplying the causal basis for calling Him rather than rivals.
Hud calls his people to worship God alone, framing the same exclusive allegiance at stake in the focus.
Salih calls his people to worship God alone and seek His forgiveness, directly uniting worship and return to God.
Shu'ayb calls his people to worship God alone, continuing the prophetic summons refused by the proud.
The true call belongs to God, while those called besides Him cannot answer, an exact conceptual parallel to the focus.
Messengers summon their people to faith, forgiveness, and respite, establishing the broader divine-call setting.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, disqualifying them as objects of worship.
People worship besides God beings that possess no provision or power, directly opposing worship of the true Lord.
At judgment the partners called by idolaters repudiate them, showing the final failure of rival invocation.
Those called besides God cannot remove or transfer harm, directly opposing effective appeal to God.
The beings people invoke themselves seek nearness to God and fear His punishment, reversing their supposed status as addressees.
When harm comes at sea, all those invoked besides God vanish from thought, leaving God as the sole recourse.
Calling upon God by His beautiful names affirms Him as the proper addressee, though response is not the point.
The companions refuse to call any god besides their Lord, explicitly joining lordship with exclusive invocation.
God commands the idolaters to call their alleged partners, who neither answer nor provide escape, directly paralleling the focus's contrast.
Abraham withdraws from false worship and says he will call upon his Lord alone.
God alone is to be worshipped and patiently served, supplying the positive alternative to pride before His worship.
God commands worship of Himself and establishment of prayer for His remembrance, a core formulation of the focus's demand.
Every messenger receives the same revelation: no god but God, therefore worship Him alone.
Abraham challenges worship of what neither benefits nor harms, reinforcing the focus's exclusive address.
Jonah calls upon God from distress and is rescued, a compact prayer-and-response counterpart to the focus.
God explicitly answers Jonah and saves him from grief, directly exemplifying the promised response.
God answers Zechariah's call and grants his request, explicitly demonstrating answered supplication.
Calling upon what neither harms nor benefits besides God is called manifest error, directly matching the focus's concern.
The one who calls a harmful, useless protector besides God chooses a disastrous relation and outcome.
God alone is the Truth, while whatever is called besides Him is false, establishing the focus's exclusive addressee.
Those called besides God cannot create even a fly and cannot recover from it, decisively exposing their incapacity.
Noah's message commands worship of God alone and denies any other god, directly echoing the focus's worship claim.
A messenger is sent to command worship of God alone and warn of the Day, linking the summons to judgment.
Calling another god beside God without proof is condemned and placed before the final reckoning.
Objects worshipped besides God neither create nor control harm, benefit, death, life, or resurrection.
On judgment day, those called besides God deny having led their worshippers astray, exposing failed dependence.
The arrogant refusal to prostrate to the Most Merciful directly parallels pride against God's worship.
God's servants do not call another god beside Him, making exclusive invocation a defining mark of faithful worship.
The introduction to Abraham's inquiry opens a sustained examination of what his people worship.
The idols neither benefit nor harm, completing the test of whether they can sustain the worship and calls given them.
The judgment question asks where the beings once worshipped have gone, exposing their absence when needed.
God answers the distressed caller, removes harm, and grants stewardship, an exceptionally close counterpart to the focus's promise.
God summons idolaters to produce the partners they claimed, exposing their failed rival address at judgment.
The repeated summons to alleged partners makes their absence at judgment a direct critique of calling them.
People are forbidden to call another god with God; all else perishes while His judgment remains.
Abraham commands worship of God, fear of Him, and obedience, stating the faithful counterpart to the focus's pride.
Those worshipped besides God cannot provide provision; people are therefore directed to seek provision from God and worship Him.
When harm touches people, they call their Lord in repentance; relief is followed by some returning to association.
Believers call upon their Lord in fear and hope while giving from provision, modeling humble devotion.
Those called besides God possess no atom's weight of power and have no share or support in creation.
The angels deny being worshipped and identify the idolaters' actual devotion to jinn, exposing false worship.
The angels disavow the worship directed to them, confirming that the claimed addressees do not accept that relation.
People take gods besides God seeking help, but those gods cannot help them, directly opposing true divine recourse.
Abraham challenges worship of what people carve with their own hands, undermining false worship.
Elijah asks whether people call on Baal while leaving the Best of creators, directly contrasting rival and true invocation.
Sincere religion belongs to God alone, while claimed intermediaries are defended as means of nearness and judged by God.
Under harm a person calls upon his Lord in repentance, then may forget the call and set up rivals after relief.
The Prophet declares that he worships God with religion sincerely devoted to Him.
Those who avoid false worship and turn back to God receive glad tidings, supplying the positive alternative.
The admission that God created all things destabilizes the later reliance on beings called besides Him.
When God alone is mentioned, idolaters recoil, but they rejoice at mention of others besides Him, closely matching resistance to exclusive address.
The Prophet rejects any command to worship other than God, making exclusive worship explicit.
God commands people to call upon Him with religion sincerely devoted to Him, an immediate and near-exact parallel to the focus.
The rival call has no valid claim in this world or the next, while return is to God and excess leads to the Fire.
The Living One is to be called with religion sincerely devoted to Him, repeating the focus's central invitation in the same surah.
At judgment idolaters are asked where their alleged partners are, immediately preceding their admission that the partners vanished.
When afflicted a person calls upon God at length, then turns away when favor comes, illustrating unstable responsiveness.
People are commanded to answer their Lord before an irreversible Day arrives, directly connecting response and final judgment.
The Prophet is instructed to ask whether any gods besides the Most Merciful were appointed for worship.
Jesus identifies God as his Lord and theirs and commands worship of Him, directly restating the focus's rightful worship.
None is further astray than one who calls besides God beings that will not answer until resurrection and are unaware of the call.
The jinn urge their people to answer God's caller for forgiveness and protection from painful punishment.
The Day of Resurrection is announced as the day the Caller calls from a near place, extending the focus's ultimate summons.
People are forbidden to set another god alongside God, grounding exclusive worship and invocation.
Places of worship belong to God, so no one is to be called alongside Him.
When God's servant stands calling upon Him, opponents crowd around, showing resistance to exclusive divine address.
The Prophet declares that he calls only upon his Lord and associates no one with Him.
No one can protect from God or provide refuge apart from Him, reinforcing sole dependence on the divine addressee.
All people are commanded to worship their creating Lord, establishing the foundational worship relation pride refuses.
Believers are commanded to worship God and give thanks to Him, stating the positive devotional response.
God is identified as Lord, Creator, and the one to be worshipped, directly grounding exclusive worship.
The Prophet is told to follow revelation from his Lord and turn away from associators, supporting the focus's exclusive allegiance.
Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are devoted to God alone, extending exclusive worship into total allegiance.
Noah calls his people to worship God alone and warns them of a tremendous Day.
Hud calls his people to worship God alone and warns that they should be mindful of Him.
Salih calls his people to worship God alone and grounds the summons in a clear sign from their Lord.
God is named as Lord, Creator, and governor, followed by the command to worship Him.
Those worshipped besides God are shown unable to harm or benefit and unable to serve as valid intercessors.
The Prophet declares that he does not worship what others worship besides God, but worships God alone.
Joseph declares that judgment belongs to God and that He commanded worship of none but Him.
The Prophet calls to God with insight, making direct divine invitation explicit.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God and not associate anything with Him, directly restating exclusive devotion.
Every community receives the command to worship God and avoid false objects of worship.
God forbids taking two gods and commands reverent fear of Him alone.
God decrees that none be worshipped except Him, placing exclusive worship at the center of obligation.
Worship of the Lord must be free of association, directly opposing the diversion of devotion to others.
God is declared Lord and people are commanded to worship Him as the straight path.
Aaron tells the people that the Most Merciful is their Lord and commands them to worship and obey Him.
God alone is identified as the deity with encompassing knowledge, countering the calf's false worship.
Believers are commanded to bow, prostrate, and worship their Lord, the humble embodied opposite of the focus's pride.
People worship besides God what neither benefits nor harms, directly describing misdirected worship.
Reliance and praise are directed to the Ever-Living God, a related posture of sole dependence.
God alone is declared deity and Lord of the supreme throne, grounding the exclusivity of worship.
Association with God is named a grave wrong, directly supporting the focus's exclusive worship relation.
The speaker declares that he should worship the One who created him and to whom all return.
Taking gods besides God is rejected because their intercession cannot help and they cannot save.
God is declared one, the central truth resisted by those proud of exclusive divine address.
Elijah identifies God as Lord and best of creators while challenging the call to Baal.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God with religion sincerely devoted to Him.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God and be among the grateful, directly stating the faithful alternative.
The Prophet is forbidden to worship what is called besides God and commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.
People are forbidden to prostrate to the sun and moon and commanded to worship their Creator alone.
Abraham dissociates himself from what his people worship, except the Creator who will guide him.
The closing command to prostrate to God and worship Him embodies the humility opposed to pride in the focus.
